All three pipelines clear 0.97 on their own validation, and the order follows what each allowed itself to use. Claude kept the account-ID batch and the donation-timing features (0.982). Gemini dropped the ID batch but kept lifetime donations and donor tenure (0.977). GPT-6 Astra dropped all three on leakage grounds (0.973). Most of the gap is on the hard group (new or lapsed patrons: 0.90 / 0.87 / 0.84), which is exactly where those features carry signal.

The more rigorous the validation, the lower the reported score. GPT-6 Astra used fully nested CV for tuning and pruning. Gemini reused the same five folds for every stage. Claude tuned once on one repeat. Only GPT-6 Astra's 0.973 is close to unbiased; the other two are mildly optimistic. The Kaggle public score is the only check none of them saw.
Claude vs Gemini is not a significant difference (−0.0045, 95% CI −0.012 to +0.003). Claude vs GPT-6 Astra is (−0.009, CI −0.017 to −0.001).

All three independently found the same core signal: recency of the last subscription, streak or continuity, and whether the patron subscribed last season. None of them proposed a neural network. Each settled on tree models plus logistic regression: GPT-6 Astra on gradient boosting, Gemini and Claude on random forest + logistic blends.

Hyperparameter tuning mattered less than expected. Gemini's tuning made its logistic and forest models worse (0.975 → 0.957 / 0.960) and it reverted to its defaults. GPT-6 Astra's nested tuning gained about +0.003. Claude's search mostly confirmed strong regularisation (shallow trees, flat sensitivity to C).

Pruning helped every pipeline, most for the model that started with the most features: GPT-6 Astra's boosting went 0.952 → 0.969 after nested pruning to 76 features. Gemini's forest gained +0.0003 (66 → 33 features) and Claude's blend about +0.001 (25 → 17).
Blending was a small, consistent win when used. Gemini +0.002 over its best single model, Claude about +0.0005. GPT-6 Astra deliberately avoided blends to keep validation clean.

They agree on who will subscribe but not on the order of everyone else. 146–148 of each model's top 150 test accounts are shared, yet rank correlations are only 0.88–0.89. The disagreement is in ordering the ~2,800 unlikely accounts, and AUROC still counts that ordering. Gemini had the best average precision (0.848): its highest-ranked accounts are the purest.

Process: GPT-6 Astra needed one fix-up round in three of its four stages and spent the most tokens, but wrote the most defensive code: nested CV, bootstrap intervals, explicit caveats. Gemini 3.8 Flash ran first time at every stage and was fast, but stalled on Google rate limits until the Antigravity route was used. Gemini 4 Argon was unavailable (OpenRouter key at $0), so Flash was substituted.

For your write-up, the decision that matters most is the leakage stance, not the algorithm: whether the account-ID batch and the 2014 donation fields are legitimate pre-season information. Two independent models judged them risky; including them is worth about 0.005–0.01 AUROC.
